power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing Need a Better Definition of "Test" 2 ßAbstract Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing determine their scope by defining a "test".
This definition is of practical consequence due to the significance of Standards for test evaluation, individual-level and policy decisions, and legal proceedings.
I argue the current version lacks sufficient clarity.

In light of the ongoing revision of the Standards, I consider the language of the current codex and its purpose, along with its predecessors, and propose a new definition of "test" that addresses the issues of the current definition -big and small -while being rooted in the contemporary approach to test validity.
The new definition helps clarify how Standards regulate different kinds of psychological and educational testing, including the anticipated rise in AI-driven assessment.
One way to ensure that psychological testing proceeds de lege artis is to agree upon, codify and enforce a set of basic requirements directed at users, developers, publishers, and policy makers.
But even when optimally drafted, such codices may prove ineffectual when their scope is set up incorrectly.
Too broad, it makes the requirements unfeasible to follow, thus eroding their authority.
Too narrow, it lets improper instances of incompetent testing evade scrutiny.
This issue raises a question familiar to legal theory -correct application of legal concepts is obvious for some real-world cases, but difficult for others.
To use Hart's ( 2012) classic example, one may wonder if a rule "no vehicles in the park" restricts roller-skates as well.
text.formatted: To use Hart's ( <ref type="formula">2012</ref>) classic example, one may wonder if a rule "no vehicles in the park" restricts roller-skates as well.

text.text: Proper framing of scope, as described above, presents an alike problem.
Therefore, we may use similar solutions.

For instance, we can construct a coherent reading of the guidelines' text to develop a reasonable interpretation of their intended scope (e.g., Scalia & Garner, 2012, Ch. "The "Fair Reading" Method").
text.formatted: For instance, we can construct a coherent reading of the guidelines' text to develop a reasonable interpretation of their intended scope (e.g., <ref type="bibr">Scalia & Garner, 2012, Ch. "</ref>The "Fair Reading" Method").

text.text: Or, just like when roller-skates might be let into the park if one can prove that the rule's purpose was to avoid high-speed vehicles, we may rely on the guidelines' purpose to serve as an interpretative aid.

In this paper, I argue that special attention needs to be given in the ongoing revision of the Standards for Psychological and Educational Testing (henceforth "the Standards") to the delineation of their scope.

I begin by interpreting the scope of the current version of the Standards (AERA/APA/NCME, 2014; henceforth "Standards 2014") based on their plain text, stated purpose, and changes between preceding versions.
Next, I critique the scope as currently defined and propose a revised version that may prove a better alternative.
Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing Need a Better Definition of "Test"

The core definition of the Standards' 2014 scope is based on the concept of "test" defined as: […] a device or procedure in which a sample of an examinee's behavior in a specified domain is obtained and subsequently evaluated and scored using a standardized process (p. 2).

"Test" is also distinguished from assessment: […] a broader term than test, commonly referring to a process that integrates test information with information from other sources. (ibid) This definition implies the following material characteristics of "tests": (1) They are devices or procedures designed to sample from a behavioral domain.
(2) Their outcome is evaluation and scoring of this sample.
(3) This process is standardized.

"Assessment" is not "test" because, according to the Standards 2014, it lacks connection to a specific course of behavioral sampling -assessment relies on extra-test information, which is not sampled but used in full.
The conclusion that assessments (described as something not anchored to behavioral samples) are not tests thus flows from the main definition.
Standards 2014 then mention additional clarifications.
And for good reason.

Read plainly, the main definition may have the Standards apply to school tests: math tests, for example, sample pupils' performance on tasks from a math knowledge domain, the outcome is scored and evaluated through grades, and everyone's test gets administered and graded the same way.
Yet, this is an area typically seen as outside of the Standards' normative pressure, and indeed even the text carves an exception.

As Standards 2014 add: the precise demarcation between measurement devices used in the fields of educational and psychological testing that do and do not fall within the purview of the Standards is difficult to identify. (p. 2) In this context, Standards 2014 mention that "rigorous application of the Standards" is "generally not possible" in "unstandardized employment assessments", "the broad range of unstructured behavior samples used in some Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing Need a Better Definition of "Test" forms of clinical and school-based psychological assessment" and "instructor-made tests that are used to evaluate student performance in education and training".

They add that [i]t is useful to distinguish between devices that lay claim to the concepts and techniques of the field of educational and psychological testing and devices that represent unstandardized or less standardized aids to day-to-day evaluative decisions. (p. 3) Here, Standards 2014 describe an out-of-scope devices and procedures by emphasizing they are "aids" which are of "day-to-day" use.
There are several ways to interpret these additions vis-à-vis the main definition.
First, they may simply constitute an interpretative guideline, as evident from the phrases "generally not possible" and "it is useful".
If deliberate choices, they may be read as general statements designed to help the reader understand the main definition.
On the other hand, they may also be seen as normative, intended to alter it.
I would argue in favor of the second reading.
Setting up a scope of a normative document and then immediately commenting on the inadequacy of the definition seems like a poor approach (see the surplusage canon in Scalia & Garner, 2012).
text.formatted: Setting up a scope of a normative document and then immediately commenting on the inadequacy of the definition seems like a poor approach (see the surplusage canon in <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Scalia & Garner, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, I find it surprising the Standards would use a criterion referring to the procedure's or device's "laying claim" on educational and psychological concepts and techniques as a simple, non-binding advice.
The Standards are obviously only applicable to "tests", however defined, at least somewhat associated with the field of educational and psychological testing.
This characteristic is completely missing from the main definition, despite being crucial.
Hence, I would conclude that at least this part of the text is intended as a part of the "test" definition.
Based on a reading favoring coherence of the entire chapter and assuming normative intent, we could extend the Standards 2014 "test" definition followingly:
Let us now consider how these two additions align with the Standards' broader context.
I discuss three major sources: the Standards' history, the Standards 2014's preface (see the prefatorymaterials canon in Scalia & Garner, 2012) and validity theory.
text.formatted: I discuss three major sources: the Standards' history, the Standards 2014's preface (see the prefatorymaterials canon in <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Scalia & Garner, 2012)</ref> and validity theory.

text.text: Council on Measurement in Education (AERA/APA/NCME) have been releasing versions of Standards since 1954, and the definition of "test" has changed between the historical revisions of the Standards.

Older versions tended to rely on a broad description of a goal (diagnosis, practical decision, prognosis) followed by a (likely non-exhaustive) list of test types that fall under the Standards' scope. Standards 1954 and 1966 (AERA/APA/NCME, 1954 , 1966) define their scope as follows: these recommendations cover not only tests as narrowly defined, but also most published devices for diagnosis and evaluation. (p. 3) Test is not defined at all, not even in the alluded-to "narrow" sense, so Standards 1954/1966 seem to refer to a broadly shared representation of the term (issue I discuss further in the closing remarks).
text.formatted: Older versions tended to rely on a broad description of a goal (diagnosis, practical decision, prognosis) followed by a (likely non-exhaustive) list of test types that fall under the Standards' scope. <ref type="bibr">Standards 1954</ref> <ref type="bibr">and 1966</ref> <ref type="bibr">(AERA/APA/NCME, 1954</ref> <ref type="bibr">, 1966)</ref> define their scope as follows: these recommendations cover not only tests as narrowly defined, but also most published devices for diagnosis and evaluation. (p. 3) Test is not defined at all, not even in the alluded-to "narrow" sense, so Standards 1954/1966 seem to refer to a broadly shared representation of the term (issue I discuss further in the closing remarks).

text.text: However, we do learn that a test's purpose is "diagnosis" or "evaluation", with "prognosis" added in Standards 1966, and that this implicit definition ought to be interpreted broadly.
text.formatted: However, we do learn that a test's purpose is "diagnosis" or "evaluation", with "prognosis" added in <ref type="bibr">Standards 1966,</ref> and that this implicit definition ought to be interpreted broadly.

text.text: Based on this, it can perhaps be claimed that right from their inception, have the Standards been intended to apply to Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing Need a Better Definition of "Test" (psychological or educational) devices of some real-world consequence.

Moreover, the publication status of the evaluated device seemed to be relevant to the determination of whether it falls under the scope (likely associated with their particular focus on test documentation; e.g., Standards 1954, p. 2).

Standards 1974 (AERA/APA/NCME, 1974, pp. 2-5) take a different angle as they are designed to apply to all assessment procedures, devices or aids, defined as "any systematic basis for making inferences about characteristics of people" (p. 2).

Test is then defined as "a special case" of assessment: a set of tasks or questions intended to elicit particular types of behaviors when presented under standardized conditions and to yield scores that will have desirable psychometric properties such as high reliability and high validity (ibid).
A non-exhaustive list of examples then follows.
Interestingly, Standards 1974 apply to assessments as well as tests, but to the first, they apply in "varying degrees".
Furthermore, they also apply to criterion measures. have happened due to a drive to make the Standards more accessible (Lennon, 1975, p. 136).
text.formatted: Furthermore, they also apply to criterion measures. have happened due to a drive to make the Standards more accessible <ref type="bibr">(Lennon, 1975, p. 136)</ref>.

text.text: Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing Need a Better Definition of "Test"
As shown above, the Standards have not been framed without considering validity theory (for historical summary see Kane and Bridgeman, 2021).
text.formatted: As shown above, the Standards have not been framed without considering validity theory (for historical summary see <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Kane and Bridgeman, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Writing about validity in the Standards, Cizek (2020, Ch. 2), speaks of the "primacy of validity".
text.formatted: Writing about validity in the Standards, <ref type="bibr">Cizek (2020, Ch.</ref> 2), speaks of the "primacy of validity".

text.text: Inquiring into Kane's (1992) approach to validity explains why Standards 2014 define validity as "the degree to which evidence and theory support the interpretations of test scores for proposed uses of tests" (p. 11).
text.formatted: Inquiring into <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Kane's (1992)</ref> approach to validity explains why Standards 2014 define validity as "the degree to which evidence and theory support the interpretations of test scores for proposed uses of tests" (p. 11).

text.text: Briefly summarized, testing helps the user make a particular decision.

This inference is warranted if the user can make a coherent, plausible argument that the test scores were correctly constructed, they can be appropriately generalized, they can be extrapolated to a non-test domain, they can be provided a theoretical interpretation and (even if all of the above holds) they can be used for a proposed decision (Kane, 1992).
text.formatted: This inference is warranted if the user can make a coherent, plausible argument that the test scores were correctly constructed, they can be appropriately generalized, they can be extrapolated to a non-test domain, they can be provided a theoretical interpretation and (even if all of the above holds) they can be used for a proposed decision <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Kane, 1992)</ref>.

text.text: How can acknowledging the close association between Kane's approach to validity, the issue of fairness and the Standards 2014 help us interpret their scope?
If we accept Cizek's (2020, Ch. 2) claim that the Standards have, both today and historically, been driven by validity, perhaps the "test" definition ought to conform to this principle as well.
In the current version, this consideration is either completely missing or integrated quite well.
The answer depends on whether you see the additional clarifications as having normative value.
Including "test score interpretation for a given purpose" and "test consequences" into the explicit definition thus appears consistent with the Standards' intent.

The stated purpose of Standards 2014 is quite neutral: to provide criteria for the development and evaluation of tests and testing practices and to provide guidelines for assessing Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing Need a Better Definition of "Test" 9 the validity of interpretations of test scores for the intended test uses.
(Standards 2014, p. 1) But the prior sentences are more revealing.

The goal of the Standards 2014 is to "promote sound testing practices and to provide a basis for evaluating the quality of those practices" because tests, properly used, can effect "better decisions about individuals and programs than would result without their use and can also provide a route to broader and more equitable access to education and employment".
While "improper use of tests […] can cause considerable harm to test takers and other parties affected by test-based decisions".
I would read this statement as emphasizing the value of "making better decisions", "preventing harm", and "inclusion and equity".
In effect, our definition of "test" should, perhaps, closely align with these values.
Of course, it is no surprise that the Standards would be framed with these values in mind, especially the latter two instances.
Anyone worth their psychometrics salt is painfully aware of the terrible role psychological and education testing has played in the discredited policies of the West (e.g., Zwick, 2021).
Fairness first appeared in Standards 1974 alongside a more explicit rebuke of specific instances of discriminatory testing practices (Sireci & Randall, 2021).
text.formatted: Fairness first appeared in Standards 1974 alongside a more explicit rebuke of specific instances of discriminatory testing practices <ref type="bibr">(Sireci & Randall, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, these maxims can perhaps be useful for interpreting and setting up the Standards' scope as well.
For instance, we may ask if the extant definition supports pursuing these values: does it avoid creating loopholes through which harmful practices can escape evaluation?

Test is (a) any device or procedure in which a sample of observations pertaining to a content domain is generated and (b) subsequently evaluated using a standardized process (c) for the purpose of making consequential decisions for an individual or for public policy, and (d) this evaluation has the potential to make a reasonable user believe that it presents evidence important for making such decision (e) by laying claims on concepts from psychological or educational theory or claiming that psychometric, machine-learning or similar techniques were used in development.
The first part (a) is left virtually unchanged from Standards 1999/2014, containing a "sampling domain criterion".
It alludes to the sampling domain theory as a framework of sufficient generality.

Unlike the preceding versions of the Standards, this approach lets the framers avoid using a list of typical test types; instead, focusing on their common material characteristic as a behavior sampler.
Similarly, part (b) overlaps with Standards 1999/2014 by defining test as a standardized procedure, creating a "standardization criterion".
Arguably, this criterion serves to distinguish between (standardized) testing and (unstandardized) assessment.

However, it surely does not mean to imply that foregoing the standardization process makes a device or procedure fall Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing Need a Better Definition of "Test" 11 outside of the Standards.
Otherwise, no procedure could ever violate the Standards as it could be claimed that lack of quality follows from imperfect standardization, hence the procedure is out of the Standards' scope.

Rather, standardization refers to test use which is broadly designed as a process in which test users follow a set of instruction that turn raw observations into scores and, subsequently, their interpretation for a given purpose.
Furthermore, the new phrasing would remove one possible source of confusion.
The Standards 1999/2014 definition speaks of "scoring and evaluation".
Does a procedure stop being a test because the behavior samples are only evaluated, not scored?
What if they are only scored and never evaluated?

Brown's (1975, p. 9-10) commentary on Standards 1974 speaks of a "descriptive" use of test, such as when tests are administered within a continuous relationship with a non-specific future use in mind.
Nevertheless, Brown concludes the Standards apply in these cases as well.

Since scores always need to be evaluated in some way to be useful for making decisions (and if not, they are of no consequence), I suggest getting rid of the scoringevaluating doublet and keeping "evaluation" only.
Part (c) contains a "purpose criterion" designed to make the purpose of the Standards explicit in the definition of "test".
In several places, Standards 1999/2014 emphasize that it is the consequences of psychological and educational testing that motivated their framing.
In other places, on the other hand, they place "day-to-day decisions" (p. 2) out of their scope.
Therefore, consequences appear to implicitly determine the Standards' scope.
The change is not without its limits, though, as it relies on another vague concept: the "consequential" qualifier.
Part (d) contains an "evidence impression criterion", an entirely new addition based on two ideas.
First, it uses the "reasonable person" standard that is typical in the law of various jurisdictions.

The standard is used to evaluate whether the test documentation presents itself (in Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing Need a Better Definition of "Test" its documentation or advertising) as if it is a psychological or educational test.
Arguably, this approach is useful to target non-scientific methods that nevertheless impress the users into thinking they have scientific value.
In other words: if the test claims authority, it needs to back it up with evidence outlined in the Standards.
The second idea of part (d) is the concept of "evidence".
Inspired by Bayesian reasoning, I propose to focus on the test user's subjective belief regarding the evidence needed to warrant a test interpretation.
For instance, a test may be designed to support binary classifications.
An assumption underlying the use of such a test is that it can meaningfully shift the pre-test odds of the target characteristic's presence in a client.
Formally, one could describe such an effect using likelihood ratios derived from sensitivity and specificity ().
Informally, a test documentation or advertising may allude to "high accuracy" and so on.
Under the proposed definition, both descriptions create an impression that the test's classification is a meaningful piece of evidence for the intended interpretation.
Therefore, the Standards would apply to both, and the informally advertised test too would have to prove its classification utility.

Part (e) introduces a "theoretical-technical claim criterion" which follows a formulation from Standards 1999/2014: devices that lay claim to the concepts and techniques of the field of educational and psychological testing (p. 2).

Because Standards 1999/2014 mention this criterion when demarcating between "tests" and "non-tests", I assume that claiming educational and psychological concepts or techniques is crucial for the Standards' scope.
Therefore, it ought to be integrated into the explicit definition.
Note that the theoretical-technical claim (e) must be connected to the evidence impression (d).
Thus, simply discussing psychological theory would not activate this clause, unless it is connected to eliciting the impression of the test's evidentiary value.

One could point out that viewing the Standards as a quasi-legal document is misguided: they were never intended to be interpreted using legal techniques, and there are several places in their text that support such perspective (e.g., on p. 7, the Standards 1999/2014 reject being interpreted as a checklist and provide other limiting statements), although there are others that counter it, such as the APA Guidelines for Psychological Assessment and Evaluation that describe the Standards as mandatory and enforceable (APA, 2020).
Yet I do not believe that subscribing to this position changes much.
The issue of scope is still there.
The unclear definition -still there.
The need to apply the Standards in a coherent and informed way?
Still there.
The only material consequence would be that quasi-legalist arguments are given less weight than this paper assigns them.
That is fair, and I would find it beneficial if our community explicated what kind of reasoning it finds convincing when interpreting the Standards.
The legalistic way is, indeed, merely a suggestion grounded in a discipline that has been grappling with similar issues for centuries.
Similar -not identical.
Another possible criticism could turn my own framing against my argument.

The opening reference to Hart's (2012) work implies that language makes it difficult to come up with perfect Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing Need a Better Definition of "Test" 14 definitions of normative concepts.
text.formatted: The opening reference to <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Hart's (2012)</ref> work implies that language makes it difficult to come up with perfect Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing Need a Better Definition of "Test" 14 definitions of normative concepts.

text.text: Hart even writes that a margin of uncertainty should be tolerated, and indeed welcomed in the case of many legal rules, so that an informed judicial decision can be made when the composition of an unforeseen case is known and the issues at stake in its decision can be identified and so rationally settled. (pp.
Perhaps a similar insight is behind the difference between Standards 1974's and Standards 1985's way of defining their scope.
Maybe this is a wise move -but I would like to see it defended against alternatives, such as the more elaborate definition proposed here, or the one used in Standards 1974.
Finally, one can be comfortable with the proposed approach but not with the new definition.
I welcome any improvement.
One way is to use the methods I show above and arrive to different, sounder conclusions.
Another way is to take an empirical approach.

My lawyer colleagues and I are exploring ways for empirically mapping the contents and structures of vague legal concepts, like judicial dignity and public order, using the social representations approach (Smejkalová, 2024;  for specific examples Palíšek et al., 2025 , Smejkalová et al., 2024).
text.formatted: My lawyer colleagues and I are exploring ways for empirically mapping the contents and structures of vague legal concepts, like judicial dignity and public order, using the social representations approach <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Smejkalová, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr"/> for specific examples <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Palíšek et al., 2025</ref> <ref type="bibr">, Smejkalová et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Social representations fit this topic.
A vague legal concept can still be a useful regulative tool because the community may implicitly agree on what situations fall under its scope and which do not.
Similarly, what "test" is, or rather, to what kind of human activities the Standards ought to apply, is perhaps represented the same way.
Test developers, users and publishers know these devices "when they see them", even if unable to properly define them.
It may be illuminating to conduct an empirical investigation into the social representation of "test" (as it pertains to the Standards' scope), and have these findings inform the new definition.
evade by claiming they use "non-tests"?
Let us make sure the upcoming revision is sensitive to this issue.

Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing Need a Better Definition of "Test" 3 Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing Need a Better Definition of "Test"
Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing Need a Better Definition of "Test" 6 Tests are (1) designed to sample from a behavioral domain.
(2) Their outcome is evaluation and scoring of this sample.
(3) This process is standardized.
(4) They lay claim to the concepts and techniques of the field of educational and psychological testing.
(5) They are more than an aid to day-to-day decisions.
Therefore, we can see that Standards 1974 present the most elaborated and expansive definition yet.
Tests are now also characterized through behavior sampling and their association with psychometric properties (reliability and validity).
Standards 1985 (AERA/APA/NCME, 1985) step away from the sprawling definition of their predecessor.
The list of examples is given prior to the following definition: "constructed performance tasks, questionnaires, and structured behavior samples".
Again, tests are contrasted with assessment, but like Standards 1999/2014, Standards 1985 seem to be written so that they do not apply to assessment.
I do not know what led to this step away from the much clearer definition in Standards 1974.
Based on a contemporary review, we can speculate that this may
Based on the above, I propose a new definition of "test" to be used in the revised version of the Standards.
Its primary aim is to make the results of the interpretation laid out above explicit in the definition itself.
I believe these changes do not alter the Standards meaning but, rather, clarify what was originally intended but left implicit.
Secondarily, I made my own Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing Need a Better Definition of "Test" changes that are additions to the original intent.
I explain the changes after introducing the new definition.
Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing Need a Better Definition of "Test" 13 Furthermore, Part (e) connects theoretical and technical claims.
The latter is especially salient due to the anticipated rise in LLM-based assessment.
Standards ought to explicitly regulate this area as to not create ambiguity as to whether LLM-based ("AI") testing needs to follow the Standards.
Discussion By now, you have perhaps, come to agree with me that the Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing need to define "test" better.
Perhaps, you even agree with my specific solution.
But my approach and the proposed definition are not without their own issues.
